claim: Intracellular membrane fusion mediates diverse processes including cell growth, division and communication.
source: Intracellular membrane fusion mediates diverse processes including cell growth, division and communication.
evidence: This is a general statement about membrane fusion that draws from established scientific knowledge in cell biology.

claim: Fusion involves complex formation between SNARE proteins anchored to adjacent membranes.
source: Fusion involves complex formation between SNARE proteins anchored to adjacent membranes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of membrane fusion involving SNARE proteins.

claim: A large number of TGN-derived membrane vesicles fuse with one another to form the partitioning membrane during plant cell division.
source: We have addressed this problem in the context of plant cell division in which a large number of TGN-derived membrane vesicles fuse with one another to form the partitioning membrane.
evidence: This statement describes the biological context of the study and is supported by established knowledge of plant cytokinesis.

claim: Blocking vesicle formation at the TGN revealed cis-SNARE complexes.
source: Blocking vesicle formation at the TGN revealed cis-SNARE complexes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental manipulation and observation.

claim: Cytokinetic SNARE complexes were already assembled at the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: These inactive cytokinetic SNARE complexes were already assembled at the endoplasmic reticulum and, after passage through Golgi/TGN to the cell division plane, transformed into fusogenic SNARE complexes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through experimental data blocking traffic at the ER.

claim: Inactive cytokinetic SNARE complexes transform into fusogenic SNARE complexes after passage through Golgi/TGN to the cell division plane.
source: These inactive cytokinetic SNARE complexes were already assembled at the endoplasmic reticulum and, after passage through Golgi/TGN to the cell division plane, transformed into fusogenic SNARE complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations showing cis-SNARE complexes at ER/TGN and their role in fusion at the division plane.

claim: Long-distance trafficking of inactive SNARE complexes ensures delivery of large stoichiometric quantities of SNARE proteins required for forming the partitioning membrane in the narrow time frame of plant cytokinesis.
source: This mode of trafficking might ensure delivery of large stoichiometric quantities of SNARE proteins required for forming the partitioning membrane in the narrow time frame of plant cytokinesis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the observed trafficking mode.

claim: Long-distance trafficking of inactive SNARE complexes would facilitate directional growth processes during cell differentiation.
source: Such long-distance trafficking of inactive SNARE complexes would also facilitate directional growth processes during cell differentiation.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to other cellular processes.

claim: In non-plant eukaryotes, a contractile actomyosin ring strongly reduces the area of contact between the forming daughter cells during cytokinesis.
source: In non-plant eukaryotes, a contractile actomyosin ring strongly reduces the area of contact between the forming daughter cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about animal cell cytokinesis.

claim: Little membrane expansion has to be supported by membrane traffic and fusion in non-plant eukaryotic cytokinesis, which can largely be afforded by local recycling.
source: Consequently, little membrane expansion has to be supported by membrane traffic and fusion, which can largely be afforded by local recycling (Nakayama, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nakayama, 2016.

claim: Dividing plant cells lack the contractile actomyosin ring.
source: In contrast, dividing plant cells lack the contractile actomyosin ring and thus have to make a large partitioning membrane – named cell plate – which is progressively formed from the centre to the periphery of the cell (Müller and Jürgens, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about plant cell cytokinesis, supported by citation.

claim: Dividing plant cells have to make a large partitioning membrane named cell plate which is progressively formed from the centre to the periphery of the cell.
source: In contrast, dividing plant cells lack the contractile actomyosin ring and thus have to make a large partitioning membrane – named cell plate – which is progressively formed from the centre to the periphery of the cell (Müller and Jürgens, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about plant cell plate formation, supported by citation.

claim: The cell plate originates from membrane vesicles that fuse with one another upon delivery to the plane of cell division along the highly dynamic microtubules of the phragmoplast.
source: The cell plate originates from membrane vesicles that fuse with one another upon delivery to the plane of cell division along the highly dynamic microtubules of the phragmoplast.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of cell plate formation in plant cytokinesis.

claim: Membrane fusion during Arabidopsis cytokinesis requires a cytokinesis-specific Qa-SNARE named KNOLLE.
source: Membrane fusion during Arabidopsis cytokinesis requires a cytokinesis-specific Qa-SNARE (aka syntaxin) named KNOLLE (Lauber et al., 1997), which forms two distinct functionally overlapping SNARE complexes by interaction with different sets of promiscuous SNARE partners
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Lauber et al., 1997.

claim: KNOLLE forms two distinct functionally overlapping SNARE complexes by interaction with different sets of promiscuous SNARE partners.
source: Membrane fusion during Arabidopsis cytokinesis requires a cytokinesis-specific Qa-SNARE (aka syntaxin) named KNOLLE (Lauber et al., 1997), which forms two distinct functionally overlapping SNARE complexes by interaction with different sets of promiscuous SNARE partners: (i) QaQbcR-complex containing Qbc-SNARE SNAP33 and R-SNARE VAMP721 or VAMP722, and (ii) QaQbQcR-complex containing Qb-SNARE NPSN11, Qc-SNARE SYP71 and R-SNARE VAMP721 or VAMP722 (El Kasmi et al., 2013; Heese et al., 2001; Zheng et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the composition of KNOLLE-containing SNARE complexes.

claim: The QaQbcR-complex contains Qbc-SNARE SNAP33 and R-SNARE VAMP721 or VAMP722.
source: (i) QaQbcR-complex containing Qbc-SNARE SNAP33 and R-SNARE VAMP721 or VAMP722
evidence: This describes the composition of one KNOLLE-containing SNARE complex, supported by citations.

claim: The QaQbQcR-complex contains Qb-SNARE NPSN11, Qc-SNARE SYP71 and R-SNARE VAMP721 or VAMP722.
source: (ii) QaQbQcR-complex containing Qb-SNARE NPSN11, Qc-SNARE SYP71 and R-SNARE VAMP721 or VAMP722 (El Kasmi et al., 2013; Heese et al., 2001; Zheng et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the composition of the second KNOLLE-containing SNARE complex, supported by citations.

claim: The formation of trans-SNARE complexes requires the cytokinesis-specific action of the Sec1/Munc18 (SM) protein KEULE.
source: The formation of these trans-SNARE complexes requires the cytokinesis-specific action of the Sec1/Munc18 (SM) protein KEULE, which interacts with monomeric KNOLLE but not with the assembled KNOLLE-containing SNARE complex at the plane of cell division (Park et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Park et al., 2012.

claim: KEULE interacts with monomeric KNOLLE but not with the assembled KNOLLE-containing SNARE complex at the plane of cell division.
source: The formation of these trans-SNARE complexes requires the cytokinesis-specific action of the Sec1/Munc18 (SM) protein KEULE, which interacts with monomeric KNOLLE but not with the assembled KNOLLE-containing SNARE complex at the plane of cell division (Park et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Park et al., 2012.

claim: The cytokinesis-specific Qa-SNARE KNOLLE is made during late G2/M phase and turned over rapidly at the end of cytokinesis.
source: The cytokinesis-specific Qa-SNARE KNOLLE is made during late G2/M phase and turned over rapidly at the end of cytokinesis (Lauber et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Lauber et al., 1997.

claim: Newly synthesised KNOLLE protein is inserted into the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and traffics along the secretory pathway via Golgi stack and trans-Golgi network (TGN) to the plane of cell division.
source: Newly synthesised KNOLLE protein is inserted into the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and traffics along the secretory pathway via Golgi stack and trans-Golgi network (TGN) to the plane of cell division (Figure 1A) (Reichardt et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Reichardt et al., 2007 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Upon cell-plate formation, KNOLLE is endocytosed and targeted via multivesicular body (MVB) to the vacuole for degradation.
source: Upon cell-plate formation, KNOLLE is endocytosed and targeted via multivesicular body (MVB) to the vacuole for degradation (Figure 1A) (Reichardt et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Reichardt et al., 2007 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Secretory traffic in Arabidopsis is insensitive to the fungal toxin brefeldin A (BFA), unlike the situation in mammals, yeast and most flowering plants.
source: Unlike the situation in mammals, yeast and most flowering plants, secretory traffic in Arabidopsis is insensitive to the fungal toxin brefeldin A (BFA).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Arabidopsis biology.

claim: BFA inhibits the ARF-activating guanine-nucleotide exchange reaction of sensitive ARF-GEFs, thus preventing the formation of transport vesicles.
source: BFA inhibits the ARF-activating guanine-nucleotide exchange reaction of sensitive ARF-GEFs, thus preventing the formation of transport vesicles (Mossessova et al., 2003; Renault et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mossessova et al., 2003 and Renault et al., 2003.

claim: A BFA-inducible system was engineered in Arabidopsis with which secretory traffic can be blocked at two specific sites along the route, ER and TGN.
source: We have engineered in Arabidopsis a BFA-inducible system with which secretory traffic can be blocked at two specific sites along the route, ER and TGN.
evidence: This describes the experimental system developed for this study.

claim: BFA-insensitive ARF-GEFs GNL1 or BIG3 were eliminated by mutation, leaving BFA-sensitive GNOM and BIG1,2,4, respectively.
source: Relevant BFA-insensitive ARF-GEFs, human GBF1-related GNL1 or human BIG1-related BIG3, were eliminated by mutation, leaving BFA-sensitive GNOM and BIG1,2,4, respectively (Richter et al., 2007, 2014).
evidence: This describes the genetic manipulation used in the study, supported by citations.

claim: BFA treatment of gnl1 mutant plants prevents recruitment of COPI coat complexes to the cis-Golgi membrane, causing collapse of the ER-Golgi traffic.
source: Consequently, BFA treatment of gnl1 mutant plants prevents recruitment of COPI coat complexes to the cis-Golgi membrane, causing collapse of the ER-Golgi traffic.
evidence: This describes the effect of BFA treatment in the gnl1 mutant, based on experimental observations.

claim: Qa-SNARE KNOLLE is retained in the ER in BFA-treated gnl1 mutant plants and cytokinesis is impaired, resulting in binucleate cells.
source: Qa-SNARE KNOLLE is thus retained in the ER and cytokinesis is impaired, resulting in binucleate cells (Figure 1A) (Richter et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Late-secretory traffic from the TGN to the plane of cell division requires the formation of AP-1 complex-coated transport vesicles, which depends on the action of four functionally overlapping ARF-GEFs BIG1 to BIG4.
source: Late-secretory traffic from the TGN to the plane of cell division requires the formation of AP-1 complex-coated transport vesicles, which depends on the action of four functionally overlapping ARF-GEFs BIG1 to BIG4 (Park et al., 2013; Richter et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Park et al., 2013 and Richter et al., 2014.

claim: Mutational inactivation of the sole BFA-resistant ARF-GEF BIG3 renders AP-1 vesicle formation BFA-sensitive.
source: Mutational inactivation of the sole BFA-resistant ARF-GEF BIG3 renders AP-1 vesicle formation BFA-sensitive.
evidence: This describes the genetic manipulation and its effect on BFA sensitivity.

claim: KNOLLE is retained at TGN membrane aggregates called BFA compartments in BFA-treated big3 mutants and cytokinesis is impaired, resulting in binucleate cells.
source: KNOLLE is thus retained at TGN membrane aggregates called BFA compartments and cytokinesis is impaired, resulting in binucleate cells (Figure 1A) (Richter et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: β-estradiol (EST)-inducible expression of KNOLLE SNARE partners NPSN11 or SNAP33 fused to a fluorescent protein was used to overcome the limitation of asynchronous cell division.
source: To overcome this limitation, we used β-estradiol (EST)-inducible expression of KNOLLE SNARE partners NPSN11 or SNAP33 fused to a fluorescent protein (Zuo et al., 2000).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study, with citation.

claim: Neither YFP:NPSN11 nor GFP:SNAP33 was expressed without EST treatment.
source: Importantly, neither YFP:NPSN11 nor GFP:SNAP33 was expressed without EST treatment (Figure 1B–C), which is a prerequisite for the detection of newly-made cytokinesis-specific SNARE complexes.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: YFP:NPSN11 and GFP:SNAP33 accumulated in TGN-containing BFA compartments in BFA-treated big3 mutant seedlings.
source: The two fusion proteins accumulated in TGN-containing BFA compartments; this was in contrast to the strong labeling of cell plates in wild-type seedlings expressing BFA-resistant BIG3 ARF-GEF or in big3 mutant seedlings not treated with BFA (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: The frequency of cells undergoing cytokinesis was not altered by BFA treatment of wild-type or mutant seedlings, as evidenced by immunostaining of phragmoplast microtubules.
source: The frequency of cells undergoing cytokinesis was not altered by BFA treatment of wild-type or mutant seedlings, as evidenced by immunostaining of phragmoplast microtubules (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and quantified in Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation analysis of BFA-treated big3 mutant seedlings expressing EST-inducible YFP:NPSN11 revealed the presence of Qb-SNARE NPSN11 fused to YFP, Qa-SNARE KNOLLE, Qc-SNARE SYP71 and R-SNARE VAMP721/722 in the anti-GFP precipitate.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation analysis of BFA-treated big3 mutant seedlings expressing EST-inducible YFP:NPSN11 revealed the presence of Qb-SNARE NPSN11 fused to YFP, Qa-SNARE KNOLLE, Qc-SNARE SYP71 and R-SNARE VAMP721/722 as well as the absence of Qbc-SNARE SNAP33 in the anti-GFP precipitate (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Qbc-SNARE SNAP33 was absent in the anti-GFP precipitate from BFA-treated big3 mutant seedlings expressing EST-inducible YFP:NPSN11.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation analysis of BFA-treated big3 mutant seedlings expressing EST-inducible YFP:NPSN11 revealed the presence of Qb-SNARE NPSN11 fused to YFP, Qa-SNARE KNOLLE, Qc-SNARE SYP71 and R-SNARE VAMP721/722 as well as the absence of Qbc-SNARE SNAP33 in the anti-GFP precipitate (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only the members of the KNOLLE-NPSN11-SYP71-VAMP721/722 complex were co-immunoprecipitated whereas the SNARE partner SNAP33 from the other KNOLLE-containing SNARE complex was not.
source: Thus, only the members of the KNOLLE-NPSN11-SYP71-VAMP721/722 complex were co-immunoprecipitated whereas the SNARE partner SNAP33 from the other KNOLLE-containing SNARE complex was not.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation analysis of big3 mutant seedlings expressing EST-inducible GFP:SNAP33 showed that Qc-SNARE SYP71 was not detected in the co-immunoprecipitate.
source: The converse was observed in the co-immunoprecipitation analysis of big3 mutant seedlings expressing the EST-inducible Qbc-SNARE member of the other KNOLLE complex, GFP:SNAP33. Qc-SNARE SYP71 was not detected in the co-immunoprecipitate, in contrast to the members of the trimeric KNOLLE complex Qbc-SNARE GFP:SNAP33, Qa-SNARE KNOLLE and R-SNARE VAMP721/722 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The members of the trimeric KNOLLE complex Qbc-SNARE GFP:SNAP33, Qa-SNARE KNOLLE and R-SNARE VAMP721/722 were detected in the co-immunoprecipitate from big3 mutant seedlings expressing EST-inducible GFP:SNAP33.
source: The converse was observed in the co-immunoprecipitation analysis of big3 mutant seedlings expressing the EST-inducible Qbc-SNARE member of the other KNOLLE complex, GFP:SNAP33. Qc-SNARE SYP71 was not detected in the co-immunoprecipitate, in contrast to the members of the trimeric KNOLLE complex Qbc-SNARE GFP:SNAP33, Qa-SNARE KNOLLE and R-SNARE VAMP721/722 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The interaction detected by co-immunoprecipitation was exclusively confined to members of the KNOLLE-containing complex that contained the EST-induced SNARE partner.
source: Thus, the interaction detected by co-immunoprecipitation was exclusively confined to members of the KNOLLE-containing complex that contained the EST-induced SNARE partner, strongly suggesting that only direct interactions between SNARE complex members were detected.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation of KNOLLE required the EST-induced expression of YFP:NPSN11 or GFP:SNAP33.
source: Further co-immunoprecipitation experiments with non-EST-induced seedlings demonstrated that co-immunoprecipitation of KNOLLE indeed required the EST-induced expression of YFP:NPSN11 or GFP:SNAP33 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mixing protein extracts with varying amounts of extract from KNOLLE::mCherry:KNOLLE transgenic seedlings before immunoprecipitation did not change the amount of KNOLLE-containing SNARE complex formed.
source: In addition, to rule out that these complexes might have formed during the immunoprecipitation procedure, we mixed the protein extracts with varying amounts of extract from KNOLLE::mCherry:KNOLLE transgenic seedlings before immunoprecipitation with anti-GFP beads. Neither 1x nor 10x mCherry:KNOLLE addition changed the amount of KNOLLE-containing SNARE complex formed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental control shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: BFA treatment did not stimulate the formation of KNOLLE-containing SNARE complexes.
source: We also addressed whether BFA treatment might stimulate the formation of KNOLLE-containing SNARE complexes. To this end, we compared protein extracts from untreated wild-type seedlings with those from BFA-treated wild-type seedlings. No obvious difference in KNOLLE complex formation was detected between treated and untreated seedlings (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: EST-induced KNOLLE-partners GFP:SNAP33 and YFP:NPSN11 did not co-immunoprecipitate the Qa-SNARE PEP12.
source: As an additional control, we examined whether EST-induced KNOLLE-partners GFP:SNAP33 and YFP:NPSN11 co-immunoprecipitated the Qa-SNARE PEP12 (aka SYP21). PEP12 is normally located at the multivesicular body (MVB) (da Silva Conceição et al., 1997; Müller et al., 2003), and was also relocated to the same BFA compartments as was YFP:NPSN11 in BFA-treated big3 mutant seedlings (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B). Neither SNAP33 nor NPSN11 interacted with mRFP-tagged PEP12 whereas both did interact with KNOLLE, confirming the specificity of the co-immunoprecipitation assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is an experimental control shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: PEP12 is normally located at the multivesicular body (MVB).
source: PEP12 is normally located at the multivesicular body (MVB) (da Silva Conceição et al., 1997; Müller et al., 2003)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PEP12 was relocated to the same BFA compartments as was YFP:NPSN11 in BFA-treated big3 mutant seedlings.
source: PEP12 is normally located at the multivesicular body (MVB) (da Silva Conceição et al., 1997; Müller et al., 2003), and was also relocated to the same BFA compartments as was YFP:NPSN11 in BFA-treated big3 mutant seedlings (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: KNOLLE forms part of a SNARE complex before the initiation of the fusion process at the plane of cell division.
source: These results indicate that KNOLLE forms part of a SNARE complex before the initiation of the fusion process at the plane of cell division.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: KNOLLE is transported as part of two different cis-SNARE complexes from the TGN to the plane of cell division.
source: Thus, KNOLLE seems to be transported as part of two different cis-SNARE complexes from the TGN to the plane of cell division. These assembled SNARE complexes comprise either (i) KNOLLE, SNAP33 and VAMP721/722 or (ii) KNOLLE, NPSN11, SYP71 and VAMP721/722.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the co-immunoprecipitation experiments at the TGN.

claim: All relevant SNARE components (YFP:NPSN11, GFP:SNAP33, KNOLLE) were detected at the ER in BFA-treated gnl1 mutant seedlings expressing engineered BFA-sensitive GNL1BFA-sens.
source: By subcellular localisation, all relevant SNARE components (YFP:NPSN11, GFP:SNAP33, KNOLLE) were detected at the ER (Figure 1D), indicating effective inhibition of traffic between ER and Golgi stacks.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1D.

claim: BFA treatment caused accumulation of γCOP in the cytosol in gnl1 mutant seedlings.
source: As an additional control, we analysed the subcellular localisation of COPI subunit γCOP, which is normally associated with the Golgi membrane whereas BFA treatment caused accumulation of γCOP in the cytosol (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) (Richter et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, supported by citation.

claim: KNOLLE already exists as part of a cis-SNARE complex in the ER.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation with anti-GFP beads of protein extracts from BFA-treated BFA-sensitive GNL1BFA-sens. seedlings revealed that KNOLLE already exists as part of a cis-SNARE complex in the ER.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on co-immunoprecipitation experiments with ER-blocked traffic.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation analysis demonstrated interactions exclusively between components within each cytokinetic SNARE complex but not between members of the two different SNARE complexes.
source: Further co-immunoprecipitation analysis demonstrated interactions exclusively between components within each cytokinetic SNARE complex but not between members of the two different SNARE complexes, ruling out recovery of non-interacting proteins from the same membrane compartment (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3A–B.

claim: KNOLLE is trafficked in two different cis-SNARE complexes along the secretory pathway from the ER to the plane of cell division.
source: Thus, KNOLLE is trafficked in two different cis-SNARE complexes along the secretory pathway from the ER to the plane of cell division.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: Cytokinetic SNARE complexes are assembled on the ER and from there delivered as cis-SNARE complexes rather than monomeric SNARE proteins along the secretory pathway, via Golgi stack and TGN, to the plane of cell division.
source: Our results indicate that cytokinetic SNARE complexes are assembled on the ER and from there delivered as cis-SNARE complexes rather than monomeric SNARE proteins along the secretory pathway, via Golgi stack and TGN, to the plane of cell division (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Cis-SNARE complexes delivered to the division plane are transformed into fusogenic trans-SNARE complexes linking adjacent membrane vesicles.
source: This implies that cis-SNARE complexes (i.e. residing on the same membrane) are delivered to the division plane where they are transformed into fusogenic trans-SNARE complexes linking adjacent membrane vesicles.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: Breaking up cis-SNARE complexes by the action of NSF ATPase normally occurs following the fusion of membrane vesicles with the target membrane.
source: Breaking up cis-SNARE complexes by the action of NSF ATPase, which normally occurs following the fusion of membrane vesicles with the target membrane (Rizo and Südhof, 2012) would result in back-folding of the monomeric Qa-SNARE to prevent re-formation of the cis-SNARE complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SNARE complex disassembly, supported by citation.

claim: SM protein KEULE interacts with Qa-SNARE KNOLLE to keep it open as a prerequisite for the formation of the fusogenic trans-SNARE complex.
source: In cytokinesis, however, SM protein KEULE interacts with Qa-SNARE KNOLLE to keep it open as a prerequisite for the formation of the fusogenic trans-SNARE complex (Park et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Park et al., 2012.

claim: Two different types of cytokinetic cis-SNARE complexes are assembled on the ER, recruited into COPII vesicles and passed on to the Golgi stack/TGN.
source: Two different types of cytokinetic cis-SNARE complexes are assembled on the ER, recruited into COPII vesicles and passed on to the Golgi stack/TGN.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 as a summary of the findings.

claim: At the TGN, cis-SNARE complexes are incorporated into AP1/CCV vesicles for delivery to the division plane.
source: At the TGN, they are incorporated into AP1/CCV vesicles for delivery to the division plane.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 as a summary of the findings.

claim: Following disassembly by NSF ATPase, monomeric Qa-SNARE KNOLLE is assisted by SM protein KEULE in the formation of trans-SNARE complexes mediating fusion of adjacent vesicles during cell-plate formation and expansion.
source: Following their disassembly by NSF ATPase, monomeric Qa-SNARE KNOLLE is assisted by SM protein KEULE in the formation of trans-SNARE complexes mediating fusion of adjacent vesicles during cell-plate formation and expansion (Park et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and supported by citation to Park et al., 2012.

claim: The cis-SNARE complex is an energetically favoured inactive form that is well-suited for transport.
source: Trafficking of cis-SNARE complexes has two major advantages: (i) the cis-SNARE complex is an energetically favoured inactive form (Jahn et al., 2003) that is well-suited for transport and also ensures equal amounts of SNARE partners being delivered to the site of action.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Jahn et al., 2003.

claim: The cis-SNARE complex ensures equal amounts of SNARE partners being delivered to the site of action.
source: Trafficking of cis-SNARE complexes has two major advantages: (i) the cis-SNARE complex is an energetically favoured inactive form (Jahn et al., 2003) that is well-suited for transport and also ensures equal amounts of SNARE partners being delivered to the site of action.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation that SNARE proteins are trafficked as complexes.

claim: The four-helical bundle of the SNARE domains is very stable, requiring ATP hydrolysis for its disassembly.
source: The four-helical bundle of the SNARE domains is very stable, requiring ATP hydrolysis for its disassembly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SNARE complex structure and stability.

claim: Because of its stability, the assembled cis-SNARE complex is physiologically inactive, not interacting with other SNARE proteins.
source: Because of its stability, the assembled cis-SNARE complex is physiologically inactive, not interacting with other SNARE proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cis-SNARE complex properties.

claim: Trafficking of cis-SNARE complexes is a highly economic strategy of meeting the sharply rising demand for membrane-fusion capacity during cytokinesis when the equivalent of about one-third of the cell surface area has to be produced in the plane of cell division in a narrow time frame of about 30 min.
source: Moreover, this might be a highly economic strategy of meeting the sharply rising demand for membrane-fusion capacity during cytokinesis when the equivalent of about one-third of the cell surface area has to be produced in the plane of cell division in a narrow time frame of about 30 min.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: In animal cytokinesis, the problem of membrane expansion is largely solved by reducing the surface area through the constriction by the contractile ring that pulls in the plasma membrane.
source: In animal cytokinesis, the problem is largely solved by reducing the surface area through the constriction by the contractile ring that pulls in the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about animal cell cytokinesis.

claim: The remaining gap in the centre of the division plane in animal cytokinesis is closed by vesicle fusion that is mediated by plasma membrane SNARE proteins present throughout the cell cycle and/or by ESCRTIII activity.
source: The remaining gap in the centre of the division plane is then closed by vesicle fusion that is mediated by plasma membrane SNARE proteins present throughout the cell cycle (Low et al., 2003) and/or by ESCRTIII activity (Mierzwa and Gerlich, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Low et al., 2003 and Mierzwa and Gerlich, 2014.

claim: Any major expansion of the eukaryotic cell surface area requires enhanced membrane fusion capacity that cannot easily be matched by the local recycling of plasma membrane-resident SNARE proteins.
source: Apart from plant cytokinesis, any major expansion of the eukaryotic cell surface area requires enhanced membrane fusion capacity that cannot easily be matched by the local recycling of plasma membrane-resident SNARE proteins whereas the long-distance delivery of inactive cis-SNARE complexes proposed here would meet the requirement.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to other cellular processes.

claim: The long-distance delivery of inactive cis-SNARE complexes would meet the requirement for enhanced membrane fusion capacity during major expansion of the eukaryotic cell surface area.
source: Apart from plant cytokinesis, any major expansion of the eukaryotic cell surface area requires enhanced membrane fusion capacity that cannot easily be matched by the local recycling of plasma membrane-resident SNARE proteins whereas the long-distance delivery of inactive cis-SNARE complexes proposed here would meet the requirement.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to other cellular processes.
